notes.meaning: Abib means the month of new grain. It falls in late March and early April, when the barley was ripening. God made it the first month of Israel's year so they would remember how He set them free from Egypt. 'By night' means Pharaoh gave them permission to go during the night, and they finished leaving in the morning.

Here 'Passover' means the whole week-long feast, not only the lamb. The Passover meal itself was a lamb or young goat. The cattle 'from the herd' were the extra sacrifices offered during the seven days. All of it had to be done at the one place God would choose, where His altar was. Matthew Henry notes that Paul calls Christ 'our Passover,' sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Unleavened bread is flat bread made without yeast. It was plain and not pleasant to eat, so it was called 'the bread of affliction,' meaning bread of hard times. It reminded Israel of their suffering in Egypt and of how fast they had to leave, with no time for the dough to rise. Remembering the escape was meant to make them grateful to God all their lives, not just during the feast.

For the whole week no yeast could be found anywhere in the land. The Passover meat had to be eaten that same night, because meat spoiled quickly in that hot climate. Both rules kept spoiling and decay far from this holy meal. Matthew Henry, following Paul, applies it to Christians: we should keep the feast free from the 'yeast' of spite and false faith.

The Passover could not be sacrificed at home in their own towns, only at the place God chose. It was a real sacrifice, and its blood had to be sprinkled on God's altar. This kept the people to God's way and stopped them inventing their own customs. One altar also held the nation together in one faith. The old writers add that the place pointed ahead to where Christ, the true Passover Lamb, would die.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars think the feasts were first held at home or at local shrines. In this view, holding them in one central place came later, through King Josiah's reforms in the 600s BC.

notes.meaning: The lamb was to be roasted and eaten at God's chosen place, not at home. Wesley and Matthew Henry take 'in the morning' to mean the morning after the seven days of the feast. Keil and Delitzsch read it as the next morning, when people went back to their lodgings in that town, still keeping the full week. 'Tents' reminded Israel of the years when they had lived in tents.

The unleavened bread was eaten through the whole feast. The seventh day is singled out as a special gathering for worship, with no work at all. Keil and Delitzsch explain that this does not shorten the feast to six days. The last day was stressed because people might be tempted to go back to work early.

Israel counted seven weeks from the start of the grain harvest. The harvest began when the first sheaf of barley was offered to God during Passover week. Seven weeks later came the Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost, which means 'fiftieth.'

At this feast each person brought a freewill offering, a gift given gladly rather than a fixed amount. It was owed to God as their King, yet each person chose how much to give. It was to match how much God had blessed their harvest. Calvin notes that remembering God's blessing helped them give cheerfully, since everything that grows comes from Him.

The feast was a time of joy before God, and no one was to be left out. Children, servants, Levites (the priestly tribe, who had no land), foreigners, orphans and widows all shared in the meals. The offerings were shared generously with friends and the poor. Calvin says true joy is found in God, like children delighting in their father's company.

Israel had once been slaves themselves. Remembering this should make them kind to their own servants and glad for their freedom. Matthew Henry notes this feast also recalled the giving of God's law at Mount Sinai, fifty days after they left Egypt. So the best way to thank God for His law is to keep it.

The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths, lasted seven days after the whole harvest was in. That meant the grain from the threshing floor and the grapes from the winepress. It began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. Calvin notes that farm work was done by then, so it was an easy time for people to travel to worship.

Again God commands joy, and again the joy must be shared with servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows. Matthew Henry says that when we rejoice in God, we should help others rejoice too. We can do that by comforting those who are sad and helping those in need.

The feast was held at God's chosen place for seven days. The verse is a promise as well as a command: God will keep blessing them, so they can be truly glad. Matthew Henry says believers can rejoice not only for what God has given but for what He has promised.

These three feasts required every man to travel to God's place of worship. Calvin says women and young children were spared the hard journey, and the fathers came on behalf of their families. Meeting often in one place kept the nation faithful and united. No one came empty-handed, but each gave only as he was able, in thanks to God. Matthew Henry says the same rule still guides Christian giving.

Each town was to have judges to decide cases and officers to carry out their decisions. Courts met at the town gate, where people gathered and business was done. Matthew Henry calls it a mercy to have justice close at hand. Calvin adds that rulers are God's servants to keep order, so they should be respected.

Judges must not twist justice or favour anyone because of who they are. They must not take bribes, because a gift clouds the mind. A bribe can make even a wise, honest judge unable to tell right from wrong. Matthew Henry says it is better not to judge at all than to judge unfairly.

The Hebrew says 'justice, justice,' and the repeated word adds strong emphasis. It means nothing but fairness, in every case and for every person alike. Calvin notes judges need this firm resolve, because favour, hatred and clever tricks so easily pull people away from what is right. Israel's life in the land depended on it.

An Asherah was a wooden pole or post standing for a Canaanite goddess. It was often set up beside the altars of Baal. Israel must not place one, or plant trees for worship, by God's altar. That would make His worship look like the worship of false gods and could draw the people into idolatry. Clarke notes God wanted His worship done openly, with nothing hidden.

A sacred pillar was a standing stone set up near altars and treated with superstitious honour, often for Baal. God hates these, because they try to show Him, who is spirit, in a physical form. Matthew Henry says nothing misrepresents God more than worshipping Him through an image. He adds that even today our hearts can set up idols of other kinds.
